The fix agent's report is solid. I'm accepting both of its judgment calls:

  • Item 1 threshold: raise against max(|S|, 1), the same scale shell_sum already uses. A pure relative threshold wrongly rejects sums that vanish exactly by symmetry.
  • Item 8 tolerance: T-matrix atol raised to 2e-14. It is backed by 3000 biased draws and consistent with what the verifier found.

  1. Yes, that was a regression, and it will be removed. From about degree 10, the new accuracy check raised errors for sums the original main computed correctly (to about 3e-8). The fix is to switch the 1D spherical sums, where Ewald loses digits, to a spectral series (a sum of cylindrical waves). That series converges fast exactly in that far-off-axis region. So these cases will return accurate values instead of errors, and must beat the original main and vanilla treams everywhere.

  2. Being fixed at the source if it's not a big job. The same switch also avoids the NaN band inside the lattice sums. The public intkambe NaN itself will be fixed if the true value is representable.

  3. Yes, it needed fixing. The gradients are part of the switch decision and must be as accurate as the values.

  4. Being fixed. Every native call will run with normal (non-flushed) floating-point handling and restore the caller's mode afterwards, and the thread pool is always started in the normal mode. Any unsafe code sits in one tiny audited module. Tests cover the exact failing cases, including a fresh process whose first call goes through JAX. The conftest workaround will be removed to prove the fix doesn't depend on it. x86-64 can be fully tested here. For ARM (macOS) I'll report exactly how far it could be checked.

  5. Yes, being fixed. That includes the part where treams-rs is worse than upstream (0.27 off or an error for shifts between about 1e-101 and 1e-160).

  6. Yes, it would blow up memory. The matrix-free solver exists for large clusters: it recomputes the particle-to-particle translations on every iteration, so memory grows only linearly with particle count. docs/large-problems.md shows 45 MiB for 512 spheres, against 640–1,368 MiB for the dense paths. Caching every pair's translation block across iterations would make memory grow with the square of the particle count again:

    • About 150 MB for 512 spheres at dipole order.
    • About 3.8 GB at lmax = 3.
    • About 10 GB at lmax = 6.

    That defeats the purpose, and for problems where it would fit, the existing dense-factor path is already the faster choice. An opt-in cache with a memory cap would be possible, but I haven't planned it unless you want it.

  7. Noted, no change.

I'd skip it. For treams-rs, pydantic adds a dependency and overhead without solving a problem the package actually has.

Why it fits poorly here:

  • The data are NumPy arrays. What needs checking is complex128 dtype, shape and finiteness. Pydantic doesn't validate arrays natively, so every field would need a custom validator anyway. That's the same code we already have, wrapped in another framework.
  • The framework namespaces carry JAX and Torch values. Inside jax.jit or grad, object fields hold tracers and tensors, not plain numbers. Pydantic models would need arbitrary_types_allowed and validators that skip traced values, and they aren't JAX pytrees. That fights the adapter design rather than helping it.
  • Rust already validates. The bindings check shapes and physical inputs at the native call, and Python checks only metadata such as bases, polarization and k0. A pydantic layer would add a third place where the same rules live.
  • Speed matters on small calls. Many calls take microseconds, and the codebase has hand-tuned fast paths for Python scalars, measured with A/B timing. Model construction and validation on every object would show up, especially in optimization loops that build objects repeatedly.
  • Dependencies stay minimal. NumPy is the only required runtime dependency, and the project rules ask to keep it that way. Upstream treams doesn't use pydantic either, so treams users wouldn't expect it.
  • Little need for serialization. Its other strength, JSON schemas and serialization, doesn't apply: model exchange goes through the existing HDF5 reader and writer.

What gives most of the benefit without it: the standard library plus one small validation module. The plan already heads that way:

  • frozen dataclasses (@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True, kw_only=True)) or NamedTuples for options and results;
  • one private _validation.py holding the few shared checks (k0, polarization, array freezing);
  • strict static typing (pyrefly), which catches most of what pydantic would catch at runtime, at zero runtime cost.

Pydantic would start to make sense if treams-rs grew a config-file or web-service interface, or another situation where untrusted structured input arrives as JSON. Nothing in the current scope does that.
